tasks.description: Sort a list of dicts by multiple keys: first by 'age' (ascending), then by 'name' (alphabetical) as a tiebreaker.
tasks.hint:
`sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p['age'], p['name']))` — tuple keys sort by first element, then second on ties.
This is how you implement multi-key sorting in Python.
Test with two people of the same age.
tasks.solution:
people = [
    {'name': 'Carol', 'age': 30},
    {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30},
    {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 25},
    {'name': 'Dave', 'age': 25},
]

for p in sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p['age'], p['name'])):
    print(f"{p['age']} {p['name']}")
tasks.walkthrough:
The key returns a pair. Python sorts by age first; when two ages tie, it falls back to comparing names alphabetically.
Bob and Dave are both 25, so Bob comes first.

tasks.description: Implement binary search: find the index of a target value in a sorted list. Return -1 if not found.
tasks.hint:
Binary search uses `low, high = 0, len(arr) - 1`.
Each step: `mid = (low + high) // 2` then compare `arr[mid]` to target.
If equal → found; if target > arr[mid] → search right half; else left half.
tasks.walkthrough:
`low` and `high` mark the part of the list still worth searching. Each step looks at the middle and throws away the half that can't contain the target.
When `low` passes `high`, nothing is left and the function returns -1.

tasks.description: Write a bubble sort function. Sort [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90] and print each pass.
tasks.hint:
Bubble sort: compare adjacent elements and swap if out of order.
Outer loop: repeat n-1 times; inner loop: compare adjacent pairs.
After each pass, the largest unsorted element 'bubbles' to its correct position.
tasks.walkthrough:
The inner loop compares neighbours and swaps them when out of order. After each full pass, one more item is in its final place at the end, so the inner range shrinks by `i`.
The `swapped` flag lets it stop early once a pass makes no changes.

tasks.description: Use Python's `sorted()` with `reverse=True` and a custom key to sort words by length (longest first).
tasks.hint:
`sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True)` sorts by length, longest first.
Combine with `reverse=True` to flip any sort order.
Test with ['python', 'is', 'amazing', 'and', 'fun']
tasks.walkthrough:
`key=len` sorts by word length, `reverse=True` makes it longest first.
Ties keep their original order, so 'and' stays ahead of 'fun'.

tasks.description: Write a function that finds the two numbers in a list that sum to a target. Return the indices.
tasks.hint:
Brute force: nested loops checking all pairs — O(n²).
Better: use a dict to store seen values: `{value: index}`.
For each number, check if `target - number` is already in the dict.
tasks.walkthrough:
As the loop visits each number, it checks whether the partner it needs has already been seen. If so, both indices are known.
Otherwise the current number is remembered and the loop moves on. One pass, no nested loops.

lesson.intro:
Sorting is something you'll do constantly, and Python's `sorted` handles nearly
every case with the right `key`. Then two classic algorithms, binary search and
bubble sort, not because you'll write them in real code, but because they show
how to think about efficiency.

sections.heading: Sorting by several things at once
sections.body:
Return a tuple from the key function. Python compares the first element,
and only looks at the second when the first is tied.
sections.code:
people = [
    {'name': 'Carol', 'age': 30},
    {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30},
    {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 25},
]
for p in sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p['age'], p['name'])):
    print(p['age'], p['name'])

sections.heading: reverse and key=len
sections.body:
`reverse=True` flips any sort. `key=len` sorts by length. Together:
longest first.

sections.heading: Binary search
sections.body:
On a sorted list you can find something by halving: look at the middle,
decide which half the target is in, repeat. A million items takes about
twenty steps instead of a million.

sections.heading: Bubble sort
sections.body:
Compare each pair of neighbours and swap if they're out of order. After
one pass the biggest item has bubbled to the end. Repeat. It's slow
(n squared) but the code is short and easy to trace, which is why it's
taught.

sections.heading: Two-sum with a dictionary
sections.body:
Find two numbers that add to a target. The slow way checks every pair.
The fast way walks the list once, remembering each number's index in a
dictionary, and asks "have I already seen target minus this?".

watch_out: Binary search only works on a sorted list. On an unsorted one it returns nonsense.
`(low + high) // 2` with `//`. Plain `/` gives a float, which can't be an index.
Swapping in Python is one line: `a[j], a[j+1] = a[j+1], a[j]`. No temporary variable needed.
`sorted()` returns a new list; `.sort()` changes the list in place and returns None.
